title: Bow, Handshake, Whistle
bigQuestion: How do different rooms show that a match is about to start?

story.title: Two Rooms, One Minute
story.kicker: Two classes start at the same time, with two different signals.
paragraphs: It is nine o'clock. In the school gym, a PE teacher lifts a whistle. She blows one short sound. The children stop and look up. Class has begun.
Across town, a judo class starts at nine o'clock too. There is no whistle. The students kneel in a line on the mat. They bow to their teacher, and the teacher bows back.
Both rooms began at the same minute. One used a sound. One used a bow. Each signal tells people the same thing: now we start, and the rules are on.
People around the world start matches in many ways. Fencers salute. Wrestlers shake hands. Boxers wait for a bell. Each room has its own signal and its own history.
story.think: What signal tells you that your class has started?

lessons.title: The Judo Bow
lessons.mainIdea: In judo, people bow when they enter the room and before a match.
reading: Judo began in Tokyo, Japan. A teacher named Kano Jigoro started his school in 1882. He called the school the Kodokan.
In many judo schools, students *bow* when they step onto the mat. Two players bow to each other before a match. They bow again at the end.
In Japan, a bow is a common way to say hello and thank you. Judo schools kept this everyday sign of respect.

words.d: bending forward to show respect; it is a common greeting in Japan
the judo school Kano Jigoro started in Tokyo in 1882

look.title: At the Edge of the Mat
look.text: Look at a line of students in white jackets. They stand at the edge of a big green mat. One by one, they bend forward a little. Then they step onto the mat.
look.prompt: What might the bow at the edge of the mat tell others?

check.q: Who started the Kodokan judo school?
check.why: Kano Jigoro started the Kodokan in Tokyo in 1882.

check.q: When do judo players bow to each other?
check.why: In many judo schools, players bow before a match and again at the end.

check.q: What does a bow show in Japan?
check.why: In Japan, a bow is a common sign of respect, hello and thank you.

lessons.title: Sumo Starts Together
lessons.mainIdea: In sumo, there is no whistle; the two wrestlers start at the same moment.
reading: Before a sumo match, wrestlers stand in the ring. Many toss a handful of salt. This custom comes from Shinto, an old religion of Japan. In Shinto, salt stands for making a place clean.
A *referee* in a bright robe watches. He holds a wooden fan. The two wrestlers crouch and face each other. They choose the moment to start together. This start is called the *tachiai*.

words.d: the person who watches a match and makes sure the rules are kept
the moment two sumo wrestlers start a match together

look.title: Salt in the Air
look.text: Look at a big wrestler at the edge of a clay ring. His hand opens. White salt falls across the ring. A man in a silk robe waits with a fan.
look.prompt: Where does the salt custom come from?

check.q: What do many sumo wrestlers toss before a match?
check.why: Many sumo wrestlers toss salt, a custom from Shinto.

check.q: What is the tachiai?
choices: the start of a sumo match
check.why: The tachiai is the moment two sumo wrestlers start together.

check.q: What does the sumo referee hold?
check.why: The sumo referee holds a wooden fan, not a whistle.

lessons.title: The Fencing Salute
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers salute each other and the referee before a bout.
reading: *Fencing* is a sport with long, thin swords. It grew from sword schools in Europe. Fencing has been in every modern Olympics since 1896.
Before a bout, each fencer gives a *salute*. They salute the other fencer and the referee. The rule book of world fencing asks for it. A fencer who will not salute can be punished.

words.d: a sport with thin swords that grew from sword schools in Europe
a sign of respect given before a match

look.title: A Rule About Respect
look.text: Before each bout, the fencers must salute their opponent, the referee and the people watching.
look.prompt: Who do fencers salute before a bout?

check.q: Where did fencing grow from?
check.why: Fencing grew from sword schools in Europe.

check.q: Who does a fencer salute?
choices: the other fencer and the referee
check.why: The fencing rule book asks fencers to salute the other fencer and the referee.

check.q: Since when has fencing been in every modern Olympics?
check.why: Fencing has been in every modern Olympics since the first one in 1896.

lessons.title: A Handshake on the Mat
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestlers shake hands before and after a match.
reading: Wrestling is one of the oldest sports in the world. Today, a world group called United World Wrestling writes its rules.
Before a match, the two wrestlers meet in the middle. They *shake hands*. After the match, they shake hands again. Then they shake hands with the other coach too.
In the United States, school wrestlers shake hands too. The handshake says, we both agree to the rules.

words.d: to hold another person's hand as a greeting or a promise
the world group that writes the rules for Olympic wrestling

look.title: Two Hands in the Middle
look.text: Look at a round mat with a circle painted on it. Two wrestlers walk to the middle. They reach out and shake hands. A referee stands close by.

check.q: When do wrestlers shake hands?
check.why: Wrestlers shake hands before the match and again after it.

check.q: Who writes the rules for Olympic wrestling?
check.why: United World Wrestling is the world group that writes wrestling rules.

check.q: What does the wrestling handshake say?
choices: we both agree to the rules
check.why: The handshake shows that both wrestlers agree to the rules.

lessons.title: The Boxing Bell
lessons.mainIdea: In boxing, a bell starts and ends each round.
reading: Boxing matches are cut into parts called *rounds*. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 made each round three minutes long. A rest of one minute came between rounds.
A person called the timekeeper watches the clock. The timekeeper rings a *bell*. One ring starts the round. Another ring ends it. Everyone in the room can hear it.

words.d: one timed part of a boxing match
the sound that starts and ends each round in boxing

look.title: An Old Rule About Time
look.text: The rounds are to be three minutes long, with one minute of rest between rounds.
look.prompt: Which is longer, a round or a rest?

check.q: What starts a round in boxing?
check.why: In boxing, the timekeeper rings a bell to start each round.

check.q: How long was a round in the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 made each round three minutes long.

check.q: Who rings the boxing bell?
check.why: The timekeeper watches the clock and rings the bell.

lessons.title: The Whistle in the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: In a school gym, a whistle is a common signal to start and stop.
reading: Many PE teachers and referees use a *whistle*. Its sound is short and loud. It can be heard across a big room.
In 1884, a toolmaker named Joseph Hudson made a famous whistle in Birmingham, England. He called it the Acme Thunderer. Referees around the world used it.

words.d: a small tool that makes a loud, high sound when you blow into it
a sound or sign that tells people what to do

look.title: Gym Marks and Dojo Marks
look.text: Picture two rooms. In the gym, a teacher blows a whistle, and lines on the floor show where to stand. In the judo room, students bow at the edge of the mat. Both rooms have marks that tell people what to do.
look.prompt: Which mark is a sound, and which mark is a move?

check.q: What did Joseph Hudson make?
check.why: Joseph Hudson made the Acme Thunderer whistle in England in 1884.

check.q: Why do gyms use whistles?
choices: the sound is loud and short
it is a kind of bow
check.why: A whistle is short and loud, so a big room can hear it.

check.q: What is a signal?
choices: a sound or sign that tells people what to do
check.why: A signal is a sound or sign, like a whistle or a bow.

lessons.title: Honoring the Teacher
lessons.mainIdea: In Muay Thai, fighters often honor their teachers before a match.
reading: *Muay Thai* comes from Thailand. Before a match, many fighters do the *wai khru*. Wai khru means paying respect to the teacher in Thai.
The fighter moves slowly around the ring while music plays. Each gym has its own way. People who watch can learn what it means. It belongs to the fighter and the gym.

words.d: a Muay Thai custom of paying respect to teachers before a match

look.title: Slow Steps in the Ring
look.text: Look at a fighter in a square ring in Bangkok. Music plays from drums and a pipe. The fighter walks slowly to each corner. He is not fighting yet. He is honoring his teacher.
look.prompt: Why might a fighter honor a teacher before a match?

check.q: Where does Muay Thai come from?
check.why: Muay Thai comes from Thailand.

check.q: What does wai khru mean?
check.why: Wai khru means paying respect to the teacher in Thai.

check.q: Who does the wai khru belong to?
check.why: Each gym has its own way; the custom belongs to the fighter and the gym.

review.q: What do many judo players do before a match?
review.why: In many judo schools, players bow to each other before a match.
In sumo, the wrestlers start together at the tachiai.

review.q: What do fencers give before a bout?
review.why: Fencers salute the other fencer and the referee.

review.q: Which sport starts each round with a bell?
review.why: In boxing, a bell starts and ends each round.

choices: a Muay Thai custom of honoring teachers
review.why: The wai khru is a Muay Thai custom of paying respect to teachers.

review.q: What do bows, bells and whistles all do?
choices: tell people a match or class starts
review.why: Each one is a signal that says now we start.
